newsitem.title: SLOVAKIA: SMALLER BANKS HIT HARD BY SLOVAK CEN BANK MOVES.
newsitem.headline: SMALLER BANKS HIT HARD BY SLOVAK CEN BANK MOVES.

text.p: Central bank moves to soak up liquidity on the Slovak money market have increased pressure on smaller banks to raise rates, threatening them with the loss of their few lucrative clients, analysts said on Thursday.

The banking sector has become highly illiquid since the central bank stopped quoting securities repo and reverse repo rates at the beginning of the year, instead holding tenders when needed for limited volumes of short-term securities repos.
But the move, analysts say, has forced rates on the interbank market -- where most smaller banks get their funds -- up to near-record levels.
This, the analysts say, is backing smaller institutions into a corner: either raise prime rates and lose customers to larger, more liquid banks, or keep rates the same but have no liquidity.

"The liquidity crunch worsens the position of banks that depend on the interbank market for financing," Ivan Benda, treasury manager at Slovenska Sporitelna, one of the market's largest participants, told Reuters.
Local commercial banks, despite interbank money market rates of about 25 percent, said they had no imminent plans to raise their prime rates, which currently range between 11 and 14.75 percent.
Analysts added the problem is exacerbated by the fact that even large Slovak companies rely mainly on short-term rollover loans to finance their operations.

"This should be a signal for the corporate community that the trend is headed towards lowering credit activities," Sylvia Majlingova, Liquidity Department Director at CSOB Bratislava, said. "Smaller banks with bigger liquidity problems will feel the (credit) pressure first," she added.

The liquidity crunch has hit the market hard in the past week, peaking on Wednesday when, for the first time, the banking sector as a whole was short of liquidity fulfilling requirements at only 97.75 percent.

An estimated three to six banks, possibly including some of the market's reference banks, were not able to fulfill reserve demands, and faced further liquidity problems since they hold few state securities to refinance their operations.
"Liquidity has become the main task of the day," Daniel Bytcanek, chief dealer at Polnobanka, told Reuters.
"But I would have rather seen the NBS re-imposing credit limits right away instead of hitting banks credit departments through treasuries and destroying the market," he added.
The NBS has said that by reducing the refinancing volumes, it hoped to help curb credit expansion which is at the heart of the country's burgeoning money supply.
Many banks said they still hoped that either the NBS would reverse the recent moves or the short-term capital flow from abroad would help to supply market with liquidity.
But NBS officials say they see no need at this point to change their current.

"The (market) situation after the moves we have made so far proves that we are going in the right direction...raising our hopes that the current moves will bring us the desired result," Peter Andresic, head of NBS Open Market Operations, said.
